title: Zeroth-order Algorithms for Distributed Online Optimization against Byzantine Edge Attacks
summary: arXiv:2511.05104v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Byzantine attacks pose a fundamental challenge to distributed optimization, especially when they occur on communication edges, where truthful and corrupted messages coexist and attacked links are difficult to identify. While most existing studies focus on time-invariant objectives, many practical systems operate in dynamic environments and require distributed online optimization under such attacks. A central question is whether sublinear dynamic regret, a benchmark performance in online optimization, can still be achieved under Byzantine edge attacks. This paper answers this question affirmatively. We directly study distributed online optimization with time-varying directed networks, where the identities of adversarial edges are unknown to the agents and may change over time, and only zeroth-order feedback is available. Two resilient algorithms are proposed based on randomized and deterministic zeroth-order schemes. The former is more query-efficient and requires weaker smoothness conditions, while the latter provides deterministic guarantees and better performance in simulations. title: Why $2$, $3$, and $5$? Lambert Series, Prime Logarithms, and a $48$-Step Octave for Musical Tuning
summary: arXiv:2611.33219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The primes $2$, $3$, and $5$ generate many familiar frequency ratios in musical tuning. We identify three mathematical properties that distinguish these primes in a construction based on modular transformations of Lambert series. We derive an exact identity for $\log p$ for every odd prime $p$, together with a separate identity for $\log2$. Within this construction, all transformed Lambert-series arguments can be chosen real precisely for $p=2,3,5$. In the identities obtained for these three primes, every series argument has magnitude at most $e^{-2\pi}$, whereas the identity for $\log7$ requires complex arguments and contains a more slowly converging series. The leading $\pi$-terms for $\log2$, $\log3$, and $\log5$ generate a $48$-step octave grid and recover its conventional prime mapping $(48,76,111)$ exactly, without rounding, while including the leading $\pi$-term for $\log7$ enlarges the grid to $1680$ steps. The identity for $\log7$ introduces no auxiliary logarithms of larger primes, whereas for every prime $11\le p<20000$, an exact computation identifies such logarithms in the construction. title: Why $(4x(1-x))^{3/4}$ approximates the binary entropy so well: a proof of Tops{\o}e's convexity conjecture
summary: arXiv:2611.33213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Write the binary entropy as $h(x) = u^{g(x)}$ with $u = 4x(1-x)$. Topsoe (2001) proved the sharp bounds $1/\ln 4 \le g \le 1$, i.e. $u \le h \le u^{1/\ln 4}$, and conjectured that the effective exponent $g$ is convex. We prove this conjecture. In the variable $s = (1-2x)^2$, $g$ extends to a Pick function on $\mathbb{C} \setminus [1,\infty)$ with an explicit positive density on the cut, so that $g(x) = \sum_n \gamma_n (1-2x)^{2n}$ with $\gamma_n > 0$ and $(\gamma_n)_{n \ge 1}$ a moment sequence. Pinelis's monotonicity theorem, Topsoe's power-type bounds and the optimality of their exponents follow as corollaries, together with a classification of all exponents $\alpha$ for which $u^\alpha$ bounds $h$. The proof is by hand except for one inequality in one real variable on a bounded interval, certified by interval arithmetic. As an application we give sharp, certified constants for the approximation $h \approx u^{3/4}$: $-0.0065493 \le u^{3/4} - h \le 0.0080004$ on $[0,1]$.
